body_html:
As I mentioned in Weekly #76, I think the odds of a much broader global conflict are rising, yet I had no aerospace and defence exposure in the portfolio.

So for my April Stock Pick, I started digging into that world. On April 13th, I sent a trade alert with my pick.

Below is the deep dive.

I will admit, this is not a cheap corner of the market anymore. The sector has already re-rated as the market woke up to the obvious: war, rearmament, and strained supply chains tend to get attention. But once you look past the headline valuation multiples, there are still a few pockets where the risk-reward looks interesting.

There are two things worth keeping in mind from the start.

First, the situation with Iran is fluid. Right now, there is a two-week ceasefire (or has the ceasefire been cancelled? Not sure anymore 🤔), but that can change quickly. The conflict could resume, escalate, or cool off. My own view is that it is more likely to continue than disappear. Still, that part is outside my control, and it is outside yours too. So I don’t want an idea that only works if the war gets worse. I want a fundamentally strong business that can hold up even if the headlines calm down and sector valuations cool off.

Second, investing in this theme does not mean buying the obvious defence prime contractors. The better opportunity can sometimes sit one level deeper in the chain. It is the same way I have approached AI and energy. Rather than chase the most crowded names, I would rather look for the picks-and-shovels businesses that supply something critical, hard to replace, and easy to underestimate. That is what led me here.

The stock market loves a clean story, and right now, aerospace and defence is one of its favourites. You have war in the background, defence budgets moving higher, a multiyear ramp in commercial aircraft production, and a supply chain that is still tight in the materials that actually matter. The company I found sits right in the middle of all of that.

This is not some generic industrial name hoping to catch a cyclical bounce. It supplies specialized materials and components that go into some of the most demanding aerospace and defence applications in the world. In several cases, it holds deeply embedded positions that are difficult to replace, not because management says so on a slide deck, but because qualification cycles are long, technical requirements are brutal, and customers cannot afford mistakes. Over the last several years, the business has reshaped its portfolio, pushed further into higher-value end markets, and materially improved margins. Management is guiding for more growth ahead, and the market has noticed. The stock is trading near its highs.

That leaves the real question. Is this still an attractive way to own a protected franchise at the center of one of the market’s strongest themes, or is it now just a great business priced as if nothing can go wrong? That is what I set out to answer.

TLDR

  • What it is: ATI Inc. [] is the leading producer of specialty titanium and nickel-based superalloys for jet engines, airframes, and defence platforms. Aerospace and defence now represents 68% of revenue.

  • The bull case: ATI sits at the center of three overlapping tailwinds. A multiyear commercial engine production ramp, surging global defence spending driven by real conflict, and a decade-long airframe replacement cycle. The business has transformed from a cyclical metals company into a specialty aerospace supplier with 19% EBITDA margins, $380M in FCF, and rising returns on capital. Qualification barriers make this franchise hard to displace.

  • The key risk: The stock trades at 29x EV/EBITDA and 39x forward earnings. The DCF model requires HPMC revenue to grow 25% annually for five years and margins to expand to 25%. If Boeing delays ramp or A&D budgets plateau, the premium unwinds fast.

  • The verdict: My DCF model produces a target price of $256 per share, implying 63% upside. The Monte Carlo simulation (5,000 runs) shows a median outcome of $267, with 75% of scenarios above $197. ATI is a BUY, but position sizing matters given the multiple.

Company History and Evolution

ATI has a corporate story with a long arc from American metals heritage to aerospace and defence materials specialist. The company traces its roots to the 1996 Teledyne-Allegheny Ludlum combination. Later milestones like the Allvac and Ladish acquisitions built the capabilities that matter most today: advanced jet-engine alloys, precision forgings, and deep process know-how.

That history matters because in aerospace materials, today’s moat is often the product of yesterday’s capital decisions. Vacuum melting expertise, forging presses, certifications, metallurgical know-how, and customer trust compound over decades. New entrants don’t just build a plant, hire a few engineers, and show up on a next-generation engine program. They need years of qualification work, proven reliability, and a reputation for producing parts that must not fail.

The more important transformation happened over the last five years. ATI went through a painful COVID-era contraction that saw revenue fall from $4.1B in 2019 to $2.8B in 2021…

…and net income swung to a $1.6B loss in 2020.

Management used that crisis to accelerate a portfolio shift. They divested lower-margin, commodity-exposed product lines and doubled down on the high-value aerospace and defence materials that carry pricing power and long-term customer commitments. The result is a business that looks structurally different from what it was five years ago.

ATI now sits in a part of the industrial economy where failure is not tolerated. Its products go into jet engines, airframes, military aircraft, missiles, and other mission-critical applications where performance under extreme heat, pressure, and stress is essential. The company still serves smaller niche markets such as medical implants and specialty energy, but its economic destiny is tied overwhelmingly to aerospace and defence.

How the Business Makes Money

ATI makes money through two reporting segments.

The High Performance Materials and Components segment (HPMC) is the value-dense franchise at the center of the bull case. It produces titanium and titanium alloys, nickel- and cobalt-based superalloys, powder alloys, and other advanced materials that are then processed into products such as bars, rods, seamless tubes, precision forgings, and machined parts. This segment includes some of ATI’s highest-value products, including the critical rotating discs used inside jet engines. In FY2025, HPMC generated about 53% of ATI’s revenue and delivered margins that reached 24.0% in the fourth quarter.

Advanced Alloys and Solutions (AA&S) is the broader segment. It produces flat-rolled products, specialty strip, stainless and other specialty alloys, and related components for aerospace and defense as well as more cyclical end markets such as industrial, electronics, medical, and energy. This segment accounted for the remaining 47% of fiscal 2025 revenue.

I think that the mix matters more than the headline revenue. In FY2025, aerospace and defence represented 68% of ATI’s sales, up from 62% in FY2024. Within that bucket, jet engines made up about 39% of revenue, airframes about 17%, and defence about 12%. That shift is important because a business weighted more heavily toward aerospace and defence tends to carry higher margins, longer-duration customer programs, and stickier qualification dynamics than ATI’s older, more cyclical portfolio. ATI has become less like a traditional metals company and more like a specialized aerospace supplier with a stronger earnings floor.

Long-term agreements reinforce that stability. ATI’s customer base includes many of the most demanding names in aerospace and defence: GE Aerospace [], Pratt and Whitney [], Rolls-Royce [RYCEY], Boeing [], Airbus [EADSF], Lockheed Martin [], and General Dynamics []. These are not casual customer relationships. They are built over years of qualification, joint development, and operational trust. Long-term agreements provide visibility, help lock in share, and make demand more durable than spot-market industrial sales.

Unit Economics and Key Value Drivers

ATI’s unit economics are driven less by raw metal prices and more by qualification intensity, process complexity, and value-added manufacturing depth. This is the key point many miss. ATI is not simply digging metal out of the ground and hoping for a good commodity price. It is producing materials and components that must meet demanding performance specifications in environments where heat, fatigue, and failure tolerance matter far more than the price of the feedstock.

The value creation happens in three stages.

  1. First, specialty melting: vacuum induction melting (VIM), vacuum arc remelting (VAR), and electroslag remelting (ESR) convert raw inputs into high-purity alloy ingots. This requires capital-intensive equipment, metallurgical expertise, and strict process control.

  2. Second, primary conversion: those ingots get forged, rolled, or extruded into intermediate forms.

  3. Third, precision finishing: the material gets turned into near-net-shape forgings, machined parts, or other components ready for assembly.

Each stage adds margin. ATI controls all three in-house for its most valuable product lines, and that vertical integration is a genuine competitive advantage.

For a material to be approved for use in a jet engine hot section, it must go through a multi-year qualification cycle that includes material characterization, mechanical testing, process audits, and flight testing. Customers like GE Aerospace and Pratt and Whitney do not switch suppliers lightly. Once a material is qualified on a specific engine program, it tends to stay qualified for the life of that program, which can span decades. This creates deeply embedded, long-duration revenue streams with limited competitive threat.

Next-generation engines use more high-performance content per unit than their predecessors. A LEAP or GTF engine contains more titanium and nickel superalloy by weight than the engines they replace, because higher operating temperatures and tighter fuel-efficiency targets demand more advanced materials. As the fleet transitions from older engines to these newer platforms, ATI’s content per engine increases. That is not a cyclical tailwind. It is a structural one.

Industry Setup

The aerospace and defence materials industry behaves far more like an oligopoly than a commodity market. A small group of integrated players controls the supply of advanced alloys and forged components that sit deep inside the value chain. The real value is created downstream in specialty melting, remelting, forging, heat treatment, testing, and precision finishing. Companies that control multiple stages of that process, like ATI, capture more value and usually hold more pricing power.

Advanced vacuum melting capacity is limited. Isothermal forging capacity is limited. Building new facilities requires significant capital, long lead times, technical expertise, and qualified labour. But the bigger constraint is procedural. Aerospace customers do not simply buy metal. They buy qualified, certified material from approved suppliers that have already proven they can deliver reliably. That makes this industry hard to enter and slow to change. When demand rises faster than qualified capacity, incumbents can stay selective, protect margins, and focus on the highest-value programs.

Three demand drivers are stacking on top of each other right now.

Driver #1. Jet engines.

Next-generation engines like the CFM LEAP and Pratt and Whitney GTF are ramping production to meet widebody and narrowbody aircraft demand. These engines use more high-performance alloy content per unit. ATI’s jet engine revenue grew 21% in 2025, and management expects double-digit growth again in 2026.

While researching this, I went back to a Veritasium video that does a great job explaining what actually makes modern jet engines so difficult to build. It is not just about engineering complexity. It is about materials. The extreme temperatures inside these engines push metals to their limits, which is where advanced superalloys become mission-critical.

Driver #2. Defence.

The US FY2026 Department of Defence budget came in at $961.6B, a 12% increase over FY2025.

That is not a one-time spike. Germany plans to reach 3.5% of GDP in defence spending. Japan approved a record $58 billion defence budget. Global defence spending hit $2.7 trillion in 2024 and is still climbing. The Iran conflict has accelerated restocking of precision munitions and spare parts, both of which require the advanced materials ATI produces.

Driver #3. Commercial airframe.

Boeing and Airbus are both working through record backlogs. Airframe inventories are expected to normalize in the second half of 2026, which should lift titanium demand. ATI recently signed a $1B, five-year titanium contract with Airbus that doubles its participation with the European airframer.

Competitive Positioning

Precision Castparts (PCC, Berkshire Hathaway) is ATI’s most direct competitor in aerospace superalloys and titanium. PCC is vertically integrated from melting to forging with deep long-term contracts across all major aerospace OEMs. Being private, PCC does not face public-market pressure on margins or growth, which gives it a different strategic posture. But it also means PCC’s capacity decisions are less transparent to the market, and its willingness to invest in new capacity is harder to track.

Carpenter Technology [] competes in premium specialty alloys, focusing on bar and wire product forms. It is a credible rival in medical and aerospace applications. CRS reported an 18.5% EBITDA margin in 2025 and is investing in its own capacity expansion, but its product range is narrower than ATI’s and it lacks ATI’s forging and component-level capabilities.

Howmet Aerospace [] competes in aerostructures and fasteners more than in raw alloys. It reported $7.4B in revenue in 2024 with a 28.8% adjusted EBITDA margin. Howmet is the best pure-play aerospace comp, but it plays in a different part of the value chain. ATI supplies the raw and intermediate materials; Howmet turns them into engineered structures.

The key competitive dynamic is that qualified capacity is tight. All of these players are running at or near full utilization in their highest-value product lines. New capacity takes years to qualify. ATI is investing in a new primary melt VIM furnace backed by long-term customer commitments and co-funding, targeting $350M in incremental revenue by mid-2028. That investment is a strong signal. Customers are willing to underwrite ATI’s capacity expansion because they need the output and cannot easily get it elsewhere.

Management and Capital Allocation

Kim Fields is President and CEO, and is set to become Board Chair in May 2026. She has led ATI through the post-COVID transformation, the portfolio shift toward aerospace and defence, and the margin expansion that has fundamentally changed the earnings profile of the business.

Capital allocation has improved materially. ATI repurchased $470M in shares during 2025, funded entirely from operating cash flow. The board expanded the buyback authorization by $500M in February 2026, bringing the total to $1.2B.

During Q4 2025, ATI also repaid $150 million in debt, reducing annualized interest expense by about $10M. There are no meaningful debt maturities until December 2027 and no planned repayments in 2026.

The balance sheet is in the best shape it has been in years. Net debt to EBITDA ended 2025 at 1.94x, down from 4.6x in 2020 and 2.7x in 2023. Total debt stands at $1.95B against $417M in cash. The company has headroom to continue investing in growth capex while returning cash to shareholders.

I like the combination of returning cash aggressively while also investing in customer-funded capacity expansion. The new nickel melt system is not speculative growth. Customers are co-funding it because they need the output. That tells you the demand signal is real and the returns on that incremental capital are likely to be attractive.

Financials: The Transformation in Numbers

The financial transformation is not subtle. In 2020, ATI generated $3.0B in revenue with a 6.7% EBITDA margin and a $1.6B net loss. In 2025, it generated $4.6B in revenue with an 18.7% EBITDA margin and $404 million in net income. That is a fundamentally different business.

Gross margin has more than doubled from 9.8% in 2020 to 22.0% in 2025. That reflects the shift toward higher-value aerospace products within HPMC and the pruning of lower-margin industrial volumes. It also reflects better operating discipline and the pricing power that comes with qualification-based customer relationships.

EBITDA margin reached 18.7% for the full year, but the Q4 ran at 19.7%, which gives a better read on the current trajectory. The 2023 dip to 12.9% reflects one-time items and operational disruptions, not a structural regression. The rebound to 18.7% in just two years confirms the underlying improvement is real.

FCF turned strongly positive at $334M in 2025, up from $168M in 2024 and negative in 2023. Operating cash flow of $614M was a record. Adjusted FCF was $380M, up 53% y/y. This is the first time in the current cycle that ATI has been able to fund growth, return cash, and strengthen the balance sheet simultaneously.

ROIC has improved to 12.7% from just 1.0% in 2020, but it still has room to run. The model projects ROIC reaching 17% in 2026 and approaching 20% by 2030 as revenue scales and margins expand.

That would put ATI’s return profile closer to a high-quality industrial compounder than a cyclical metals business.

Valuation: What the DCF Model Says

My DCF model stress-tests whether the current price reflects fair value or if there is still upside to capture. The model produces a target price of $256 per share, implying 63% upside.

View the DCF Model Here

Key Assumptions

HPMC revenue growth of 25% annually for five years is the most consequential assumption. It is grounded in three observable drivers: jet engine production rates ramping with higher ATI content per unit (engine revenue +21% in 2025), a contracted $1B Airbus titanium deal plus new nickel melt capacity targeting $350M in incremental revenue by mid-2028, and a multi-year defence spending upswing driven by real conflict.

EBITDA margins expand from 17.2% in 2025 to 21.7% at the terminal. HPMC is modelled at 25% (management has already demonstrated 24% in Q4 2025) and AA&S at 16% (below the 16.3% achieved in 2025). The expansion comes from operating leverage and continued mix shift toward higher-value products.

WACC of 6.6% is derived from: risk-free rate 4.38%, market risk premium 4.23%, levered beta 1.38, cost of equity 10.2%, cost of debt 3.56%, and an optimal debt-to-capital ratio of 55%.

DCF Valuation Bridge

The terminal value represents 82% of the total enterprise value, typical for a growth business with strong competitive positioning. The exit EV/EBITDA implied by the terminal assumptions is approximately 15.9x, reasonable for a specialty aerospace materials franchise with secular demand tailwinds.

Monte Carlo Simulation (5,000 Runs)

The median outcome of $267 implies 71% upside from the current price. Even the 25th percentile outcome of $197 is 26% above the current price, meaning that in a below-average scenario, the odds still favour making money.

The simulation varies five inputs simultaneously using normal distributions. HPMC revenue growth is centred at 20% with a 5 percentage point standard deviation, meaning roughly two-thirds of scenarios fall between 15% and 25%. That range captures both the base case and a world where Boeing delays or defence spending softens.

HPMC EBITDA margin is centred at 25% with the same 5-point spread, reflecting the uncertainty around whether Q4 2025's 24% margin is the floor or the ceiling.

AA&S revenue growth is set at 3% with a 3-point standard deviation, and AA&S margin at 16.5% with a 3-point spread. Both are intentionally tight because AA&S is the slower-moving segment and contributes less than 1% of total variance combined.

WACC is centred at 6.6% with a 1.5-point standard deviation, which lets the simulation explore a range from roughly 3.6% to 9.6%. That last variable dominates everything.

WACC alone explains 61.8% of the variance in the output, followed by HPMC revenue growth at 26.3% and HPMC margin at 11.5%. The takeaway is clear: the thesis lives or dies on two things — what discount rate the market assigns to this business and whether HPMC can keep compounding.

A quick aside. I built this Monte Carlo simulator myself. The Google Sheets extension I had been using was too rigid: limited variables, slow, and the output told me less than I wanted to know. So I wrote my own. It runs up to five variables simultaneously, supports more distribution types, executes faster, and produces cleaner output. I liked the result enough that I wanted to share it for free. I submitted it to the Google Marketplace, and it was rejected without explanation. I plan to sort that out over the coming weeks when time allows, but if you have experience with this and want to help, let me know!

What the Market is Pricing In

The implied WACC at the current price is approximately 6%, assuming my DCF cash flow projections are correct. That is below my base case of 6.6% and suggests the market is either pricing in a lower discount rate environment or more optimistic growth. Alternatively, the defence-sector sentiment premium has pushed the multiple beyond what the fundamentals alone justify.

The implied growth rate at the current price is 12% annually for the next 10 years (holding WACC at 6.6%). That is high but defensible given ATI’s guidance and the secular tailwinds in both engines and defence.

Key Risks, Bear Case, and What Breaks the Thesis

Valuation compression is the most immediate risk. At 29x EV/EBITDA and 39x forward earnings, ATI is priced for continued strong execution. If growth disappoints, the multiple contracts. This is not a stock with a margin of safety at current prices. It is a stock with high expected returns if the thesis plays out and meaningful downside if it does not. The Monte Carlo 5th percentile of $124 implies 21% downside, and that is not an extreme scenario.

Boeing production delays are a real and recurring threat. Boeing’s production ramp has been delayed before and could be delayed again. If 737 MAX and 787 production rates don’t reach the targets that underpin airframe demand, ATI’s titanium volumes would fall short. Management expects airframe normalization in the second half of 2026, but Boeing has a track record of pushing timelines to the right. The $1B Airbus contract partially offsets this, but Airbus has its own supply chain constraints.

Defence spending could plateau. The current surge in global defence budgets is driven partly by real conflict and partly by political will. If the Iran ceasefire holds and broader geopolitical tensions ease, the urgency behind defence spending could fade. Defence represented 12% of ATI’s revenue in 2025. A slowdown here would not kill the thesis, but it would remove one of the three growth drivers the model depends on.

The HPMC growth assumption is aggressive. The DCF model projects HPMC revenue growing 25% annually for five years. That would take HPMC from $2.4B in 2025 to $9.3B by 2031. Maintaining that trajectory requires flawless execution on capacity expansion, no disruptions from the new nickel melt system, and continued strong demand from all three end markets (engines, defence, airframes) simultaneously. If any one leg weakens, the aggregate growth rate drops and the valuation case softens.

Raw material cost inflation could squeeze margins. Titanium sponge prices, nickel prices, and energy costs all feed into ATI’s cost structure. While long-term agreements include price adjustment mechanisms, there can be timing mismatches. In periods of rapid input cost inflation, margins could compress before price adjustments catch up.

Interest rates matter more than usual. WACC explains 62% of the variance in the Monte Carlo simulation. If the rate environment moves against ATI (higher risk-free rates, wider spreads), the terminal value shrinks and the stock price follows. At a WACC of 8%, the DCF produces a target of just $170, which is close to the current price.

Customer concentration adds fragility. GE Aerospace and Pratt and Whitney together likely represent a substantial portion of HPMC revenue. While those relationships are deeply embedded, any disruption to a single major customer program could have an outsized impact.

Variant Perception: What the Market is Missing

The market sees ATI as an aerospace and defence play trading at a full multiple. That much is priced in. What I think the market underestimates is the duration and compounding nature of the competitive advantage.

This is not a stock that will benefit from a one-time defence budget increase and then mean-revert. The qualification barriers ATI holds are structural. A competitor cannot take ATI’s position on a GE9X engine program or a Pratt GTF platform without years of qualification work and tens of millions in testing and certification costs. These positions are essentially locked in for the life of each engine program, and engine programs run for decades.

The market also appears to underestimate the margin trajectory. The HPMC segment is demonstrating that higher aerospace mix, vertical integration, and operating leverage can push EBITDA margins toward 25%. That is closer to a specialty industrial franchise than a metals company. If ATI sustains or expands margins as revenue grows, the earnings power of this business three to five years from now will be far larger than the current consensus implies.

The third edge is the customer-funded capacity expansion. When customers co-fund your capex because they need your output, the return on invested capital on that incremental capacity is likely to be well above average. The $350M in incremental revenue from the new nickel melt system will likely come at attractive margins because it is being built to fill an identified demand gap, not speculative capacity. This dynamic is more typical of a toll-booth business than a commodity producer.

Finally, the implied WACC analysis suggests the market may be anchoring to ATI’s historical identity as a cyclical metals company and applying a higher risk premium than the current business deserves. A specialty aerospace materials franchise with 19% EBITDA margins, contracted revenue, and rising ROIC should command a lower discount rate than the ATI of 2019.

Verdict

ATI is a buy. The simplest way to frame this: ATI sells into markets where demand is locked in by contracts and physics, not by consumer sentiment or ad budgets. Jet engines need specialty alloys. There is no substitute, and there are only a handful of qualified suppliers. That is not a growth story. That is a toll booth on a runway that gets longer every year. You are paying for a business that has not yet shown the market what its margin structure looks like at full capacity. I think the next two years will do that.
